concepts.title: Affinity-Based Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Affinity-based segmentation uses a distance metric to group similar patterns into segments, often by learning embeddings where high-affinity data points are clustered together.
concepts.content:
Affinity-based segmentation methods are based on the idea of affinity, where a distance metric models whether two items should be grouped. This metric usually measures how similar two patterns are or how likely they are to be part of the same object. For example, a simple affinity function over pixel pairs could be the Euclidean distance between their color values. Pixels with high affinity should belong to the same group, while pixels with low affinity should belong to different groups. Methods using this idea include graph cuts, spectral clustering, and Markov random field (MRF)-based clustering.

In modern practice, contrastive learning is a common way to implement this approach. Contrastive methods learn an embedding in which data points with high affinity are nearby and those with low affinity are far apart. Once this embedding is learned, clustering can be performed using a simple quantization method like $k$-means. This entire pipeline is shown in (see figure: Image segmentation using $k$-means over DINO @caron2021emerging features), using DINO as the particular contrastive embedding.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional clustering often struggles with complex visual data. Affinity-based segmentation provides a way to define similarity (affinity) specifically for the task, allowing for more flexible grouping. By leveraging contrastive learning, we can automatically learn these similarity metrics from data, making segmentation more robust than using simple hand-defined pixel distances.

concepts.title: Edge Detection
concepts.one_liner: Edge detection aims to create a compact representation of an image's content using sparse, stable boundaries that relate to scene geometry.
concepts.content: Edge detection is an early vision technique based on the idea that edges form a good, compact representation of an image's content. Edges are relatively sparse and remain stable despite nuisances like noise and lighting. Different kinds of edge structures are connected to scene geometry; for instance, an edge representing an occluding contour indicates a depth discontinuity at that location in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Raw pixel data is redundant and sensitive to noise. Edge detection extracts the most essential structural information, providing a stable foundation for understanding scene geometry and object boundaries.
concepts.recap_md: - Edges provide a sparse and stable representation of image content.

concepts.title: Occluding Contour
concepts.one_liner: An occluding contour is an edge that indicates a depth discontinuity in a scene.
concepts.content: An occluding contour is a specific kind of edge structure that represents a boundary where one object blocks another. In terms of scene geometry, the presence of an occluding contour indicates that there is a depth discontinuity at that location.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding which edges represent object boundaries versus surface markings is crucial for depth perception and navigating a 3D environment.

concepts.title: Line Drawings
concepts.one_liner: Line drawings represent the edge structure of an image and are highly intuitive for human perception.
concepts.content: Line drawings are a way of representing the edge structure in an image. They are of high interest to humans, suggesting that representing images via edge structure is a useful approach. While there is research in computer graphics regarding the modeling of line drawings, it remains unclear if this representation will eventually be as compelling for machine vision as it is for human vision.
concepts.motivation_md: Humans can recognize complex objects from just a few strokes. Studying line drawings helps researchers understand the minimal information required for visual recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - Line drawings capture the essential edge structure of an image.

concepts.title: Layer-Based Representation (2.5D)
concepts.one_liner: Layer-based or 2.5D representations capture aspects of depth by modeling the world as a series of layers rather than a full 3D space.
concepts.content: Layer-based representations are used in computer vision to capture aspects of depth without the computational expense of modeling a fully 3D world. These layers, and other related pseudo-3D representations, are often referred to as 2.5D representations.
concepts.motivation_md: Full 3D modeling is often computationally expensive and unnecessary for tasks like occlusion handling. 2.5D layers provide a middle ground that captures depth relationships efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - Layer-based representations are also known as 2.5D representations.

concepts.title: Ordinal Structure
concepts.one_liner: Ordinal structure refers to the relative ordering of objects, such as which item is on top of another.
concepts.content: Ordinal structure refers to the relative depth ordering of objects rather than their exact positions in metric space. For example, in a pile of paper, the ordinal structure tells us which piece is on top, which is often the most important information for interaction.
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world tasks, knowing the exact distance to an object is less important than knowing its relative order (e.g., 'A is in front of B').
concepts.recap_md: - Ordinal structure captures the relative depth ordering of objects.

concepts.title: Emergent Groups
concepts.one_liner: In modern vision systems, perceptual structures like objects and contours often emerge within hidden layers rather than being explicitly designed.
concepts.content: While explicit edge detection and bottom-up segmentation are less common in modern computer vision, perceptual organization remains present. Current systems still process the world in terms of objects, contours, and layers, but these structures are emergent in their hidden layers rather than being made explicit by human design. For example, object detectors have been observed to emerge inside neural networks trained for tasks like colorization.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why classical vision topics are still relevant: even if we don't program them explicitly, deep learning models often 'rediscover' these fundamental structures to solve complex tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Perceptual structures emerge naturally in the hidden layers of neural networks.

key_passage.text: But this doesn't mean that perceptual organization is absent from current systems. These systems still see the world in terms of objects, contours, layers, and so forth, but those structures are emergent in their hidden layers rather than made explicit by human design.

motivation.text: Edge detection and bottom-up segmentation are not the workhorses they once were. But this doesn't mean that perceptual organization is absent from current systems.

concepts.title: Perceptual Group
concepts.one_liner: A perceptual group is a visual representation where primitive elements are organized into meaningful structures like contours or objects.
concepts.content: A perceptual group is a particular kind of visual representation. While a camera sees raw RGB pixel values, the human mind sees structures such as contours, surfaces, objects, and events. (see figure: A few kinds of perceptual organization in the human visual system.) Many of these perceptual structures can be thought of as groups of primitive elements: a contour is a group of points forming a line, and an object is a group of parts forming a cohesive whole. Identifying these meaningful groups is a longstanding area of interest in both human and computer vision.
concepts.motivation_md: Grouping raw pixels into higher-level structures is necessary for an agent to understand and interact with the world in terms of objects and events rather than just light intensities.
concepts.recap_md: - Perceptual groups organize primitive elements into cohesive wholes like objects.

key_passage.text: Many of these perceptual structures can be thought of as *groups of primitive elements*: a contour is a group of points that form a line, an object is a group of parts that form a cohesive whole, and so on.

concepts.title: Why Group?
concepts.one_liner: Grouping provides a powerful substrate for downstream analysis by discovering language-like structures from unsupervised principles.
concepts.content: Grouping is a special case of representation learning, and the reasons to group are the same: groups provide a good substrate for downstream analysis and processing. Perceptual organization—the identification of objects, relationships, shapes, and events—is similar to describing an image in text. While mapping images to text is a common trend, perceptual organization aims to discover these language-like structures from bottom-up grouping rules and unsupervised principles rather than human-language supervision. Furthermore, perceptual groups can go beyond the limits of language, representing coherent structures in our minds that may be hard to name. (see figure: How many objects do you see?)
concepts.motivation_md: By discovering structure without explicit supervision, grouping allows for the emergence of semantic concepts like 'object' from raw data, facilitating reasoning and communication.
concepts.recap_md: - Grouping serves as a foundation for high-level reasoning and downstream tasks.

concepts.title: Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities.
concepts.content: Segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities. There is no single definition of what constitutes a coherent entity; it varies by task and could correspond to a nameable object, a material region, or a distinct piece of geometry (see Figure 1.1.6). Segmentation can be framed as a clustering problem where each pixel is assigned to one of $k$ clusters. Two common approaches include assigning similar pixels to the same cluster or assigning pixels to the same cluster if no boundary exists between them. (see figure: There are multiple ways you might segment any given image, and each way will highlight different world properties. concepts.motivation_md: Segmentation simplifies image analysis by breaking down a complex scene into its constituent parts, allowing algorithms to process individual objects or regions independently.
concepts.recap_md: - Segmentation partitions an image into task-dependent coherent regions.

concepts.title: K-Means Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: K-means segmentation partitions an image by clustering pixels based on their color features.
concepts.content: $K$-means is a simple clustering algorithm that can be applied to image segmentation. To use it, each pixel is treated as a datapoint and its color is used as its feature vector. For example, using $ab$ color values allows an image to be represented as a scatter plot of color distributions. (see figure: Different regions of coherent color in the image correspond to clusters in the scatter plot of all the $ab$-values of the image's pixels. In general, segmentation can be reduced to the problem of...) The algorithm finds clusters in this color space and assigns each pixel to a cluster based on its color. (see figure: $K$-means segmentation on the fruits example.) This approach effectively segments regions of constant color, such as a zebra from its background, but it fails to group complex patterns that are not defined by color similarity. (see figure: (top row): $k$-means segmentation succeeds on a seemingly hard image. *Photo source*: Fredo Durand. (bottom row): $k$-means fails on an image that, to our eye, looks no more complex.)
concepts.motivation_md: K-means provides a computationally efficient baseline for segmentation by exploiting the fact that many objects are characterized by relatively uniform color distributions.
concepts.recap_md: - K-means segments images by clustering pixels in a color feature space.

key_passage.text: K-means tries to find clusters in this scatter plot (and, if you prefer a probabilistic interpretation, it can be thought of as fitting a mixture of Gaussians to the datapoints, which aims to approximate the distribution from which these pixels were sampled). We can segment via k-means by simply assigning each pixel to the cluster assignment of its color value.

prereq.rationale: This concept explains the functional utility and motivation for forming perceptual groups.
Representing the world as layers is a specific approach to segmenting an image into depth-ordered components.
Ordinal structure provides the depth ordering that is the primary information in layer-based representations.
Layers are cited as one of the perceptual structures that emerge within the hidden layers of neural networks.
Segmentation is defined as the process of partitioning an image into regions that represent coherent perceptual entities.
K-means is presented as a primary, simple technique for achieving image segmentation.
Affinity-based methods represent a major class of techniques for solving the segmentation problem.

overlay.rationale: Line drawings provide a concrete demonstration of how image content can be effectively represented using only edge structures.
The text contrasts the emergent nature of modern perceptual structures with the explicit design of classical edge detection.
